newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Coffee eyes $1,640, cocoa cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Coffee eyes $1,640, cocoa cloudy.

text.p: Volatile coffee futures may make another assault toward $1,640 basis May this week after last week's failure to hold the eight-month peak.

With an eye on the firm New York's equivalent market, traders said London was poised to maintain some upward potential after a month-long rally which raised values by more than 30 percent since the start of the year.
One trader said that every time the market falls on correction, it picks up further steam to move higher again.
Origins were said to be well sold in the nearbys while some major roasters were reported to be short and were likely to boost their physical and price coverage.
Commodity funds are holding sizeable long positions and they could dampen the market if they decide to liquidate their positions.
Elsewhere, cocoa may bounce slightly after a dive to 18-month lows last week but traders said the market's outlook remained murky.
In sugar, the market's attention is expected to centre on expiry of the spot March on Thursday.
Coffee may draw strength from scale-up buying from roasters, which are being forced to lock in prices on the perception that the prolonged rally showed little signs of abating.
The roasters which have all this while avoided holding expensive inventories are stepping up purchases to cover their short positions and help replenish low stocks.
The high bean prices have translated into higher cup prices for drinkers but analysts warned that the roasters should try to keep the retail price hike at a minimum to avoid consumer resistance.
On the supply side, traders said the current long Tet New Year holidays in Vietnam were likely to limit large sales from the origin.
Any robusta origin sales will be met in the meantime from African sources but traders said while Ivorian sales had been good, the quality of beans was below average.
African producers decided to meet on February 26-27 to make quota allocations after agreed export curbs in Rio last month.
The market will also be eyeing a threatened strike in Colombia on Tuesday where more than 800,000 state workers are pressing for a 21.5 percent pay rise.
In cocoa, strong sterling and signs of an ample West African crop dealt a blow to prices last week as funds raided the market, selling aggressively against thin buying.
Benchmark May contract lost five percent on Wednesday, denting the market's upside prospects after a brief rally a week earlier.
Prices recouped some of the losses on Friday but traders and analysts said a drive towards 850 stg was still likely while industry buyers remained on the sidelines.
Sterling's strength against European crosses makes London an attractive sell for origins.
Traders were also disappointed by West African arrival figures which showed no sign of tailing off.
But some traders said the market's weakness could be an opportunity for bargain-hunters.
"We are convinced that investing in the upside potential of the market will pay handsomely," said traders Sucden.
In white sugar, attention should be centred on the last few trading days before the expiry of the spot March on Thursday.
But the main question will be the amount of physical delivery as trade houses have been active buyers while the market saw record turnover last week, mainly due to the large number of AAs trade.

"There is a prospect that there could be a big tonnage," said one trader, adding that Polish 60 ICUMSA sugars were again expected in the total delivery although the bulk of the tendered sugar would be from the EU.

With the raws market edging its way higher the chances of significant moves on the nearby arbitrage were slim, especially as trade sellers are hovering above the market at around $71 and above, market sources said.
Prices should also be supported by the increased physical offtake, with Iran expected to re-enter the market to buy a cargo of April white sugar after cancelling last week's tender, they added.
